text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The computer industry is the fastest growing in Sweden with total salaries increasing by 65 percent in the 1990s to 13.2 billion crowns last year, according to income and labour market research by Temaplan and Statistics Sweden.
- Swedish savings surged by 32 billion crowns in the first quarter of the year, more than during the full year 1996.
- Unions are still fighting new labour market legislation which is intended to make the labour market more flexible.

- Procter & Gamble does not want its foreign managers in Sweden to pay lower tax than their Swedish counterparts because the company believes it could cause resentment between foreign and Swedish employees. The Swedish government is looking into lowering taxes for key staff who only stay in the country for a limited time after large companies, such as telecoms group Ericsson, said they were looking into moving headquarters abroad, partly because of the high tax pressure.
- Swedish banks should be able to invest more of their reserves in listed stocks, the head of a government appointed committee preparing new bank industry legislation says.

- If Finance Minister Erik Asbrink fails to privatise state-owned Nordbanken this year, Sweden may still be able to lower the public debt enough to qualify for participation in the European monetary union.
- The task of designing a logotype for the new bank which will result from the merger of Foreningsbanken and Swedbank has been assigned to Swedish advertising guru Lars Hall.
